ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, the horizontal conveyor belt is moving clockwise at a speed of $v=6\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$. The distance between the two drive wheels $M$ and $N$ is $L_{1}=10\mathrm{m}$. If a object with mass $m=3\mathrm{kg}$ is gently placed on the conveyor belt directly above wheel $M$ (taking $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$).

1. Given that the coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and the conveyor belt is $\mu{=}0.3$, how much work is done by the frictional force of the conveyor belt on the object as it is transported from point $M$ to point $N$?
2. The conditions of problem (1) remain unchanged. If the conveyor belt speed is adjusted to $v^{\prime}{=}9\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$, find the work done by the frictional force of the conveyor belt on the object.
3. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and the conveyor belt is $\mu^{\prime}{=}0.1$, how much work is done by the frictional force of the conveyor belt on the object?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: Both attached figures show the same horizontal conveyor belt device; the conveyor belt goes around the left driving wheel M and the right driving wheel N. The block is placed at the left end of the upper conveyor belt, that is, directly above wheel M. In the middle of the upper conveyor belt there is a velocity arrow v, directed to the right, indicating that the upper belt moves from M toward N. Reasoning: The block being “gently placed” means the initial velocity is 0. In the horizontal direction, only the frictional force of the conveyor belt does work on the block, therefore by the kinetic energy theorem W_f = ΔK = 1/2 m u_N^2. When the block slides relative to the conveyor belt, it is subject to kinetic friction, whose magnitude is μmg, and acceleration a = μg; when reaching N, the velocity is taken as u_N = min(v_belt, sqrt(2 μ g L)). 1. μ=0.3, v_belt=6 m/s, a=0.3×10=3 m/s^2. The distance needed to accelerate to 6 m/s is s = v^2/(2a)=36/(6)=6 m, less than L=10 m, so before reaching N it has already reached the same speed as the conveyor belt. W_f=1/2×3×6^2=54 J. 2. μ=0.3, v_belt=9 m/s, a=3 m/s^2. The distance needed to accelerate to 9 m/s is s=81/(6)=13.5 m, greater than 10 m, so when reaching N it has not yet reached the same speed. u_N^2=2aL=2×3×10=60, W_f=1/2×3×60=90 J. 3. μ'=0.1, according to the original conveyor belt speed 6 m/s, a=0.1×10=1 m/s^2. The distance needed to accelerate to 6 m/s is s=36/(2)=18 m, greater than 10 m, so it slides throughout the whole process. u_N^2=2×1×10=20, W_f=1/2×3×20=30 J.

raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: Both attached figures show the same horizontal conveyor belt device; the conveyor belt goes around the left driving wheel M and the right driving wheel N. The block is placed at the left end of the upper conveyor belt, that is, directly above wheel M. In the middle of the upper conveyor belt there is a velocity arrow v, directed to the right, indicating that the upper belt moves from M toward N.

In the horizontal direction, only the frictional force of the conveyor belt does work on the block, therefore by the kinetic energy theorem W_f = ΔK = 1/2 m u_N^2. When the block slides relative to the conveyor belt, it is subject to kinetic friction, whose magnitude is μmg, and acceleration a = μg; when reaching N, the velocity is taken as u_N = min(v_belt, sqrt(2 μ g L)).

1. μ=0.3, v_belt=6 m/s, a=0.3×10=3 m/s^2. The distance needed to accelerate to 6 m/s is s = v^2/(2a)=36/(6)=6 m, less than L=10 m, so before reaching N it has already reached the same speed as the conveyor belt. W_f=1/2×3×6^2=54 J.

3. μ'=0.1, according to the original conveyor belt speed 6 m/s, a=0.1×10=1 m/s^2. The distance needed to accelerate to 6 m/s is s=36/(2)=18 m, greater than 10 m, so it slides throughout the whole process. u_N^2=2×1×10=20, W_f=1/2×3×20=30 J.
